name: Northwest Ridge / PCT approach
approach: From the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead (end of FR-2150, elev. ~4,600 ft), start on Trail 96 (Snowgrass Flat Trail). The first stretch climbs gently through forest for roughly 2 miles to a junction with the old Bypass Trail/Trail 96A (stay right on 96 for the more direct, less eroded line). Around 2.4-2.6 miles in you'll hear and then reach the springs that form the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right - the last reliable, easy water source before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek itself; there's no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except during heavy snowmelt, when it can run fast enough to require care. Just beyond the ford (~3.9-4 miles, ~5,800 ft) the trail breaks out of forest into the open heather meadows and wildflower bogs of Snowgrass Flat, a scenic rest and water-filter stop before the climb — note that camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself under Gifford Pinchot wilderness regulations (36 CFR 261.58(e)); parties camp instead at designated sites above/below the flats. Continue past the Trail 97 junction (west to Cispus Basin/PCT) and the Trail 86 junction (Goat Lake), staying on the main track as it climbs in long benches with Mount Adams and the Goat Rocks opening up behind you. At about 4.7 miles the trail meets the Pacific Crest Trail at roughly 7,100 ft; turn right (north) onto the PCT. Follow the PCT north for about 1.8 miles, traversing rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill terrain on Old Snowy's west flank - snow patches can linger here into midsummer and may require an ice axe/traction for a secure traverse in early season. Watch for an unmarked climbers' path branching right (east) off the PCT toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge; take it and switchback steeply uphill for about a half mile. Many parties stash poles here for the final scramble: the last few hundred feet to the 7,880 ft summit are Class 2-3 hand-and-foot scrambling on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rockfall kicked down by parties above are the main hazard on this final pitch, so avoid stacking directly below other climbers. Total one-way distance is approximately 7.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain; round trip is roughly 15.5 miles, typically taking 8.5-9.5 hours car to car.

approach_variants.name: Snowgrass Flat, the PCT north, and the unmarked climbers' path to the northwest ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead at about 4,600 ft at the end of the forest road, start on Trail 96. It climbs gently through forest roughly 2 miles to a junction with the old bypass trail — stay right on 96 for the more direct, less eroded line.

Around 2.4 to 2.6 miles you reach the springs at the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right, the last easy water before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek; there is no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except in heavy snowmelt.

Just beyond the ford at about 3.9-4 miles and 5,800 ft the trail breaks into the open heather meadows of Snowgrass Flat. Camping is prohibited within the flat itself under wilderness regulations; parties camp at designated sites above or below it.

Continue past the two trail junctions to the PCT at roughly 7,100 ft and turn right, north. Follow the PCT about 1.8 miles across rocky, increasingly exposed sidehill on Old Snowy's west flank.

Round trip is roughly 15.5 miles with about 3,600 ft of gain, typically 8.5 to 9.5 hours car to car. The access road has taken washout damage in past winters, so confirm before driving.
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-Jul through Sep, most reliable in August
hazards: An unmarked, easily missed turn off the PCT — the route's one real navigation problem
A persistent snowfield on the PCT traverse below the summit, firm and icy in early morning
Loose rock and talus on the summit scramble, with rockfall risk to climbers below
High wind and lightning exposure on an open crest, with common afternoon thunderstorms
Route-finding difficulty in poor visibility once off the PCT
Unreliable cell coverage throughout the wilderness
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The turn off the PCT is unmarked, and it is the only thing on this route you can get wrong.

The test that works in fog is about motion, not landmarks: the PCT here is sidehilling — traversing across the slope. The climbers' path is the first thing that turns uphill and stops contouring, branching right, east, toward a rocky saddle on Old Snowy's northwest ridge. Take the first thing that climbs.

The negative is equally mechanical: if the PCT starts descending on the far side of the mountain, you have walked past the turn. Go back; do not climb straight up from where you noticed.

Distance cross-check: about 1.8 miles north of the Trail 96 junction at 7,100 ft, and the path switchbacks steeply for about half a mile from where you leave the trail.

Second marker, and it sits before the turn rather than after it: a persistent snowfield on the PCT below the summit lingers into July and is a well-documented trouble spot on the exposed sidehill traverse. Meeting it means the turn is still ahead of you. It is firmest and safest crossed in the morning.

A soft confirmation at the saddle, worth knowing because it is visible from a distance: many parties stash trekking poles there for the scramble. A cache of poles on a rocky saddle is a good sign you are at the right one.

Base of the scramble: the last few hundred feet to the summit is Class 2-3 hands-and-feet on loose rock, moderately exposed but not technical. Loose talus and rock knocked down by parties above is the hazard, so do not stack directly below other climbers.

And a negative that is about visibility rather than ground: once you leave the PCT there is no maintained tread. Poor visibility is the recorded route-finding difficulty on this peak, and the honest response is to turn round at the PCT rather than to search for the spur.

itinerary.cal: Best mid-July through September; the PCT sidehill traverse below Snowgrass Flat often holds snow into July, and a free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead.

days.note: From the Snowgrass Flat trailhead (4,600 ft), climb through forest on Snowgrass Trail #96 into the flower meadows of Snowgrass Flat, then join the PCT and follow it north to the saddle below Old Snowy's west flank. Leave the PCT on a boot path and scramble loose Class 2 terrain to the summit, then reverse the entire route to the car.

itinerary.totalNote: A long single day car-to-car: about 14 miles round trip, 3,600 ft gain, typically 8-9.5 hours including a summit break.

descent_text: This is a walk-off, not a technical descent - there is no rappelling on the standard northwest ridge/PCT route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 2-3 scramble off the summit block (the loose scree and blocky talus here is the descent crux - go slow, test holds, and stay alert for rock knocked loose by parties above or below you), then pick up the climbers' path back down to the PCT. From the PCT junction, follow the trail back south, again watching footing on any lingering snowfields on the exposed sidehill traverse below the ridge (these are firmest and safest to cross in the morning before they soften). Continue south on the PCT to the Trail 96 junction (~7,100 ft) and descend Trail 96 the way you came - back through Snowgrass Flat, across the Snowgrass Creek ford, past the spring/water source, and down through forest to the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead. No ropes, anchors, or rappel gear are needed for this route under normal summer conditions; a rope and basic glacier/snow travel gear are only warranted for early-season attempts with significant snow cover on the PCT traverse or summit scramble.

pitch_detail.notes: ~4.7 mi, gentle forest and meadow hiking to the Pacific Crest Trail.
Follow PCT around Old Snowy's west/south flank, gaining benches with Adams/Goat Rocks views.
Unsigned spur path off PCT high point; loose rock, mild exposure in the final ~50 ft to the true summit.

beta: From the Snowgrass Flats trailhead, hike ~4.7 miles through forest and meadows to the PCT, then follow the PCT north/west around the mountain's flank to its high point. Leave the PCT on an unsigned boot path that switchbacks up scree/talus to the northwest ridge and follows it south to the summit; the last ~50 feet is loose Class 2–3 rock with real but manageable exposure. An alternate line gains the col between Old Snowy and Ives Peak and follows the ridge crest/just-south-of-crest to the top.

waypoints.name: Snowgrass Flats Trailhead (#96)
waypoints.note: Trail 96 begins here on FR 2150; Northwest Forest Pass required and self-issue Goat Rocks Wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at the end of Forest Road 2150, at about 4,600 feet, where the Snowgrass Flat Trail (#96) begins. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and a free self-issue Goat Rocks Wilderness permit is available at the trailhead kiosk. The access road has taken washout damage in past winters, so confirm current conditions before driving in.

waypoints.name: Snowgrass Flats meadows
waypoints.note: Trail 96 opens into heather meadows and wildflower bogs with reliable creek water; camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself per Gifford Pinchot wilderness regulations (36 CFR 261.58(e)) — use designated sites above/below the flats instead. Trail 86 splits here toward Goat Lake.

waypoints.name: Trail 97 junction
waypoints.note: Trail 97, the bypass trail, forks west here toward Cispus Basin; stay on Trail 96, which continues up through the meadows to the PCT.

waypoints.name: PCT junction
waypoints.note: Trail 96 tops out on the Pacific Crest Trail; turn north and climb a series of open benches with views of Mt. Adams and the Goat Rocks crest.

waypoints.name: Old Snowy climbers'-path junction
waypoints.note: Unmarked junction where an unmaintained climbers' path leaves the PCT for Old Snowy; many parties stash trekking poles/packs here before the scramble.

waypoints.name: Summit scree/talus scramble
waypoints.note: Final ~0.5 mi/350 ft leaves the tread for loose scree and talus with a short Class 3 hand-climbing section; watch for rockfall dislodged by climbers above and lingering steep snow into early summer.

waypoints.name: Old Snowy Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit (7,880+ ft); panoramic views of Mt. Adams, Mt. Rainier, Mt. St. Helens and the McCall, Conrad and Meade Glaciers, with Packwood Glacier visible just below to the northwest.
